name: cut
one_line: remove sections from each line of files
plain: `cut` keeps only chosen columns of each line: fields separated by a character, or character and byte positions.
It is the quick way to pull a column out of a CSV, /etc/passwd, or a log when awk is more than you need.
when: Pull one column from a CSV or log.
Keep characters 5 to 10 of every line.

examples.title: A field with a delimiter  (-d, -f)
examples.explain: -d: says the separator is a colon, -f1 keeps field 1. The result is the list of usernames.

examples.title: Several fields  (-f1,3 or -f1-3)
examples.explain: Commas pick separate fields, a dash picks a range. The output keeps the original delimiter between fields.

examples.title: From a field to the end  (-f2-)
examples.explain: A trailing dash means 'field 4 and everything after it'.

examples.title: Character positions  (-c)
examples.explain: Keeps characters 1 to 8 of each line. Good for fixed-width text.

examples.title: Everything except a field  (--complement)
examples.explain: Keeps all fields except those listed.

examples.title: Change the output separator  (--output-delimiter)
examples.explain: Replaces the delimiter in the output so it reads better.

examples.title: Lines without the delimiter  (-s)
examples.explain: -s drops lines that do not contain the delimiter. Without it such lines are printed whole.

options.plain: Use DELIM instead of the tab character as the field separator (one character).
Do not print lines that do not contain the delimiter.
Select everything except the chosen fields or characters.
Use STRING between output fields instead of the input delimiter.
With -b: do not split multi-byte characters. (Ignored by GNU cut, kept for compatibility.)
Lines end with a NUL byte instead of a newline.

mistakes: cut only accepts a single-character delimiter and splits on every one: spaces separated by several spaces make empty fields; use awk for 'any amount of whitespace'.
cut cannot reorder fields: -f3,1 still prints 1 then 3.
try: Print the home directory (field 6) of every user in users.txt.
Print the usernames of users with a bash shell using grep and cut.
Extract the date part of each log line with -c.
see_also: awk(1), paste(1), tr(1), sed(1), column(1), sort(1) -k.
captured_with: Examples are written to explain a technique; they are not captured output.
